transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we got most of the folks. I'm Maya from Redwood, account lead. We got Ethan (SE) and Sara from product security.
[00:18] Priya Anand: Hi, Priya here, thanks. We're very focused on the security posture for any private deployment.
[00:27] Ethan Patel: hi priya, thanks for the time. quick agenda: soc2/iso artifacts, rbac and sso options, audit logs to your siem, kms/hsm integration, and then network deep dive incl ingress/egress and firewalling.
[00:43] Mark Reynolds: sounds good. we also want to validate egress policy — we can't have outbound to public internet except certain endpoints.
[00:51] Sara Lopez: understoood, we'll go through how Redwood Private supports egress whitelisting and proxy + NAT patterns.
[01:05] Daniel Kim: quick note — we run a transit gateway with strict route tables, and we do centralized egress via proxies. any required external calls need to go through our proxy.
[01:19] Maya Chen: perfect, we'll surface options. Ethan, want to start on SOC 2 and ISO?
[01:25] Ethan Patel: sure — Redwood is SOC 2 Type II, we have ISO27001 attestation for the platform layer. Sara, correct me if I garbled anything.
[01:34] Sara Lopez: that's right; for Private deployments we provide a limited set of SaaS control plane artefacts, and we have a contract addendum for customers who require full on-prem control plane. Our docs include scope, third-party subservice orgs, and example evidence. Sometimes the naming in the doc generation gpt — like our tool sometimes shows Redwood Priva, small transcription quirk — but the artefacts are standard.
[01:57] Priya Anand: okay, we will need the SOC 2 bridge letters and the ISO scope and list of controls. retention for logs is important — we have to retain for at least 7 years for certain events. can you support custom retention to push to our SIEM?
[02:15] Sara Lopez: yes — audit logs can be streamed via secure forwarder to your SIEM (we support syslog over TLS, S3 with server-side encryption, and direct API ingest). retention in your SIEM is under your control. Redwood can also provide a second copy to your customer-managed S3 bucket in the same region for residency.
[02:38] Mark Reynolds: how granular are the logs? we need token-level request and response metadata (not content) along with model version, route, region, and API key id.
[02:49] Ethan Patel: we emit structured audit entries with request metadata: timestamp, request_id, model_id, model_version, user_id, source_ip, and response_status. we avoid storing content in audit logs by default — content retention is configurable and encrypted at rest.
[03:05] Daniel Kim: about encryption — we use our KMS (we prefer customer-managed keys). what's the flow?
[03:12] Sara Lopez: we integrate with customer KMS via an AWS KMS CMK or external HSM. For Redwood Private in a VPC, keys can be in the customer's account; Redwood has limited ability to see plaintext keys. keys are used to encrypt persisted artifacts (checkpoints, caches, logs) and in transit uses TLS 1.2/1.3. For air-gapped on-prem we support HSM integration — Luna and cloud HSMs tested.
[03:37] Priya Anand: great. can we require HSM for production?
[03:40] Sara Lopez: yes, we can require HSM-backed CMKs and have an operational runbook for key rotation and emergency key revocation.
[03:49] Maya Chen: ok moving into networking — Ethan you'll take the lead here?
[03:54] Ethan Patel: yep. so at a high level Redwood Private can be deployed in two patterns: 1) customer VPC with peering/transit gateway where Redwood pods run in your account, or 2) customer-connected private tenancy where Redwood manages compute in a dedicated account but network is tightly controlled via VPC peering and proxy egress. both support strict NACLs and security group boundaries.
[04:23] Mark Reynolds: we prefer the customer-account model because we need full network control. latency matters for inference though — will peering introduce jitter?
[04:33] Ethan Patel: peering is native within the cloud region and latency is minimal; we recommend colocating compute in the same AZs to reduce cross-AZ hops. we also support colocated dedicated nodes for high throughput.
[04:47] Daniel Kim: ingress — we can't accept arbitrary inbound from the internet. what's your recommended pattern for external API traffic?
[04:55] Ethan Patel: recommended pattern is to front with your API gateway or ALB in your VPC. Redwood can expose private endpoints (internal NLB) that your gateway calls over VPC peering or interface endpoints. we do not require inbound security group openings to the public internet.
[05:15] Priya Anand: what about control plane callbacks? any outbound phone-home?
[05:21] Sara Lopez: the control plane calls home are optional. For fully air-gapped we can operate a local control plane; for managed private we need limited outbound to our control plane endpoints for metrics and updates — this can be proxied and whitelisted. We publish a small set of CIDR/hostnames you can whitelist.
[05:40] Mark Reynolds: show me a list; we'll only allow proxy plus port 443 to the cert-managed endpoints.
[05:47] Ethan Patel: we'll send the exact list after the call as part of the network diagram pack.
[05:54] Daniel Kim: firewalling specifics — do you rely on security groups only or do you recommend NACLs and WAF?
[06:01] Ethan Patel: defense-in-depth: use SGs for instance-level permissions, NACLs for subnet-level whitelist, and optionally WAF for application-layer filtering. for model serving ports we typically expose only ephemeral ports to the internal NLB and allow only the gateway subnet.
[06:17] Priya Anand: egress control — we need to prevent data exfiltration. how do you handle outbound dependencies like model updates or telemetry?
[06:25] Sara Lopez: model updates can be disabled. Telemetry is configurable; you can forward metrics to a local metrics endpoint or proxy. If you require zero outbound, choose the on-prem air-gapped option and we will coordinate an offline model/package install process.
[06:42] Mark Reynolds: about host-level hardening — are nodes joined to our patching system? access via bastion?
[06:48] Ethan Patel: we support running nodes in your account so you can apply your AMI hardening and patching. SSH access is via a bastion and we use ephemeral session management; Redwood does not store long-lived SSH keys.
[07:02] Priya Anand: tell me about RBAC and SSO — we need SAML with SCIM provisioning and fine-grained RBAC where engineers can't access production keys.
[07:11] Sara Lopez: Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning for user lifecycle. RBAC is role-based and you can map groups to roles. For key management, we have policies that restrict key usage to specific service principals; production keys can be scoped so only the infra team can decrypt. We also support attribute-based access controls in our private console for fine-grained entitlements.
[07:35] Daniel Kim: can we enforce MFA?
[07:37] Sara Lopez: yes, enforced by your IdP. Redwood respects IdP session policies.
[07:42] Mark Reynolds: audit logs flow — we want immutable logs shipped to our SIEM and S3 with server-side encryption, plus KMS-protected copy for additional controls.
[07:51] Ethan Patel: the common pattern is: 1) logs written locally then forwarded to a customer-managed S3 bucket (KMS CMK), 2) a copy forwarded to your SIEM via syslog over TLS or via the S3 ingestion path, 3) we maintain an append-only audit store for short-term troubleshooting.
[08:12] Priya Anand: do you support signed audit entries for non-repudiation?
[08:16] Sara Lopez: we can enable signed entries (HMAC) for critical audit events. we also provide tamper-evidence via write-once object lifecycle to S3 where legal holds can be applied.
[08:30] Mark Reynolds: latency question — adding encryption and proxies will increase p95. do you have quant numbers?
[08:38] Ethan Patel: encryption at rest has negligible token runtime cost. proxy egress adds network hop latency; we benchmark typical added latency at 5-15ms roundtrip inside same region. for strict p95 SLOs, we recommend colocated compute and direct peering.
[08:54] Daniel Kim: what about firewall rules example? can you show standard NACL and SG templates?
[08:59] Ethan Patel: yes, for security groups: allow inbound from gateway subnet on port 443 to internal NLB; allow management CIDR from bastion only on 22/5985 (as required), all outbound blocked except to proxy on 443. NACLs: deny all inbound/outbound except ephemeral high ports and proxy ports. we'll include templates.
[09:22] Priya Anand: data residency — backups and logs must stay in eu-west-1. can Redwood ensure that?
[09:28] Sara Lopez: absolutely — for Private we can keep storage and backups in the customer account/region. even managed dedupe or cache blobs can be configured to use your regional S3.
[09:38] Mark Reynolds: monitoring and alerts — do you integrate with PagerDuty?
[09:42] Ethan Patel: yes, metrics and alerts can be pushed to your Prometheus/Grafana stack or to PagerDuty via webhook. we also support Datadog.
[09:53] Daniel Kim: network test/validation — can we run a pen test?
[09:57] Sara Lopez: yes, we welcome pen tests under a standard scope. for production windows we'll coordinate with our security team and provide IP ranges and a test account.
[10:09] Maya Chen: at a high level sounds like alignment. any other hard blockers?
[10:14] Priya Anand: key one is egress control and ability to use our HSM; second is audit log retention and signed entries.
[10:21] Sara Lopez: both feasible. for HSM we'll provide runbook and for signed logs we'll enable HMAC and push to your S3 with object lock.
[10:33] Mark Reynolds: please be explicit about the minimal outbound hosts and ports we need to allow. we can't accept wildcard DNS.
[10:40] Ethan Patel: agreed — we'll publish a host list and CIDR ranges. for managed control plane it's ~6 FQDNs and <10 /24 ranges — exact numbers will go in the diagram pack.
[10:55] Daniel Kim: related — do you support VPC endpoints for control plane so traffic stays in our backbone?
[11:01] Ethan Patel: we support interface endpoints and private link options in major clouds; traffic will remain on the provider backbone. this is the recommended path for minimal internet exposure.
[11:16] Priya Anand: about compliance artefacts — Sara, will you own delivering the packages?
[11:20] Sara Lopez: yes, I'll package SOC 2 summary, ISO scope, data flow diagrams, and KMS integration docs. Expect in 3 business days.
[11:30] Maya Chen: great. let's talk about the lab test — Mark, Daniel, what's your availability next week?
[11:36] Mark Reynolds: next week Tues and Thurs morning ok.
[11:39] Daniel Kim: Thurs morning better for me.
[11:42] Ethan Patel: we'll provision a test VPC and run a controlled ingress/egress scenario with your proxy and measure p50/p95.
[11:50] Priya Anand: one more Q — how do you handle data deletion requests under regs?
[11:56] Sara Lopez: we support purge APIs and the ability to delete customer blobs within their S3 in the same region. We provide a deletion certificate as evidence. For backups with legal holds we coordinate per customer policy.
[12:12] Mark Reynolds: good. any vendor lock-in concerns? we need exit procedures.
[12:16] Maya Chen: Redwood provides export tooling to snapshot model configs, prompts, and logs; we also have a support plan for data handoff and a documented checklist.
[12:27] Daniel Kim: let's recap next steps — Maya?
[12:30] Maya Chen: recap: Sara will send compliance docs; Ethan will send VPC/network diagram and egress whitelist; Gateway will share IP ranges and proxy details; schedule lab for week of 2026-03-23.
[12:43] Priya Anand: ok thanks all. we'll review docs on arrival and follow up on any closure items.
[12:50] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with calendar invite for the lab and attachments. end call.
[62:00] (call ended)
